description: We are a team of Computer Science students passionate about software development, UI/UX design, and space technologies. We are tackling the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts" challenge to build an innovative, user-friendly health monitoring system for astronauts during space missions. Our goal is to blend technical precision with practical solutions for human space exploration.
summary: Suha (السُّها) is a health monitoring app for astronauts on long space missions, named after the faint star in the Big Dipper that Arab astronomers used as an eyesight test. In space, health problems start as faint signs: a few short nights, a rising heart rate, a low mood. Suha gathers vitals from a smartwatch and smart suit, sleep, mood and radiation into one calm screen with a green/yellow/red status. It raises explainable alerts automatically, each linked to a NASA Human Research Program risk, so astronauts can evaluate and act on their health without waiting for Earth. It includes two doctors (a flight surgeon and a psychologist), an SOS button, a crew tracker that finds the nearest crewmate when a beacon signal is lost, a Mars mode that simulates the communication delay, and a full Arabic/English interface. It runs on the web and installs on any phone as a mobile app. All data is simulated, and Suha never diagnoses.
details:
What it does

Suha helps astronauts notice small health changes early and act on them, even far from Earth.

Astronaut: a daily check-in (sleep, fatigue, mood, stress, disorientation); vital signs that arrive automatically from a smartwatch and smart suit (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure, balance, exercise, food and water); 7- and 30-day charts; a radiation card with daily dose and mission total; a clear green/yellow/red status; and a "Suha noticed" daily summary.

Automatic, explainable alerts: Suha watches trends (for example, short sleep on 2 of the last 3 nights) and raises alerts by itself. Every alert shows why it appeared, a safe next step, and the related NASA Human Research Program risk. Suha never diagnoses.

Crew safety: an SOS button that shares readings and location; a crew tracker based on wearable beacons that alerts the crew, doctors and Mission Control automatically when a signal is lost during a spacewalk, and shows the nearest crewmate.

Two doctors: a flight surgeon (physical health) and a psychologist (mental health), each with their own dashboard, alerts, weekly printable report and private chat ("Wasl"). Mood is shared only if the astronaut agrees.

Mars mode: simulates the 3–22 minute message delay to Earth, showing how Suha keeps working onboard when the doctor cannot answer right away.

Ask Suha: an in-app assistant that answers in Arabic or English from the app's data, takes actions, and refuses to diagnose.

Devices: pair, sync and manage the smartwatch, smart suit and a sleep ring (simulated Bluetooth).

Everyone on Earth: general users can track their own health or learn in the Space Academy (5 levels, 2 mini games inspired by docking and spacewalks, a certificate, and links to real NASA learning opportunities).

Why it matters

On long missions astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in themselves. Suha turns scattered signals into one clear picture, speaks up before small problems grow, and supports body and mind together.

How it is built

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no external libraries, hand-made SVG charts and art, a rule-based alert engine, a full Arabic right-to-left interface, and a Progressive Web App (installable on phones, works offline after the first visit). Hosted on GitHub Pages. All crew members and readings are fictional and simulated.

Future plans

Real wearable data, a real AI model behind Ask Suha through a secure server, medical review of alert rules with flight surgeons and psychologists, app store release, and live astronaut sessions in the Space Academy.
